le.why: 了 after the verb says the action is done.

le.en: He isn't a student any more.
le.why: 了 at the end of the sentence says something is different now.

le.ch: 下雨了，我们不去商店了。
le.en: It's started raining, so we're not going to the shop now.
le.why: Both 了 mark a change: it's raining now, and the plan changed.
没有 says it didn't happen, so there is no 了.
了 goes right after the verb for a finished action.

de.why: 的 joins the owner to the thing: 我朋友的猫.

de.en: I want to buy the big one.
de.why: Describer + 的 can stand for the thing itself.
With close family you can drop 的: 我女儿.
For things (not family), keep 的: 我的书.

de.en: This is the fruit we bought yesterday.
de.why: 的 goes between the describer (昨天买) and the noun.

ma.why: Add 吗 to a statement to make a yes/no question.

ma.en: Is there a hospital around here?
ma.why: Keep statement order and put 吗 at the end.

ma.en: Do you have a dog at home?
How are you getting to Beijing?
ma.why: 怎么 is already a question word, so it never takes 吗.

ma.en: Does your school have Chinese teachers?
ma.why: 吗 goes at the very end; the word order doesn't change.

shi.why: 医生 is a noun, so it is linked with 是.
A + 不是 + B: 不 goes right before 是.
北京人 is a noun, so 是 is right here.
漂亮 is an adjective, so drop 是 and use 很.
不是 is one unit: 是 comes right after 不.

hen-adj.why: 高兴 is an adjective: it takes 很, not 是.
很 sits right before the adjective.
Subject + 很 + adjective, with no 是.
An adjective needs no 是; a light 很 goes in front.

hen-adj.en: The clothes here are all pretty.
hen-adj.why: 很 goes right before the adjective, after 都.

noun-pred.why: A date needs no verb, but the negative brings back 是: 不是.
In the negative a price takes 不是 before the number.

noun-pred.en: It's two in the afternoon now.
noun-pred.why: A time can follow the subject directly, no verb needed.
An age can't take plain 不; the negative needs 不是.
号 follows the day number; the date needs no 是.

you.why: The negative of 有 is always 没有, never 不有.

you.en: There's a hospital behind my home.
you.why: Place first, then 有, then what is there.
Place + 有 + thing asks what is there.

you.en: I don't have any Chinese friends.
you.why: 有 only takes 没: 没有.

you.en: There are lots of Chinese films on my computer.
you.why: Place (电脑里) + 有 + what is there.

shenme.why: You bought a thing, so ask with 什么 where the answer goes.
什么 + noun stays in the answer's place, after the verb.
什么 can go right before a noun: 什么水果.

shenme.en: What do you want to watch?
shenme.why: Keep statement order: 什么 goes after the verb, not at the front.

shenme.en: What work does your dad do?
shenme.why: 什么 sits where the answer would go, before the noun 工作.

shei.why: The one who wants tea is a person, so the question word is 谁.
谁 is the subject here, so it comes first, like the answer would.
谁的 asks whose; no 吗 is needed.
谁 already makes a question, so drop 吗.

shei.en: Who did you go to the film with yesterday?
shei.why: 谁 goes where the person's name would go: 和 + 谁.

na-nar.en: Which one do you want to buy?
na-nar.why: Which one = 哪 + measure word; 哪儿 means where.
在 + 哪儿 asks the place, and it comes before the verb.
在 + 哪儿 asks the place, before the verb.
Which one is 哪个; 哪儿 only asks where.
哪儿 goes after 在, where the place would go.

ji-duoshao.why: Prices always use 多少: 多少钱.

ji-duoshao.en: How many students does your school have?
ji-duoshao.why: A big number takes 多少, and it can drop the measure word.

ji-duoshao.en: How many books do you want to buy?
ji-duoshao.why: A small number takes 几 plus a measure word: 几本.

ji-duoshao.en: How many friends do you have?
ji-duoshao.why: 几 must have a measure word: 几个.

ji-duoshao.en: How many Chinese friends do you have?
ji-duoshao.why: 几 goes right before the measure word 个.

duoda.en: How old is your dad this year?
duoda.why: For a grown-up, ask 多大; 几 and 多少 need a measure like 岁.
几岁了 asks the age of a child or a pet.

duoda.en: How old are you, little one?
duoda.why: Talking to a child, 几岁 is just right.
几 means 'how many', so it needs 岁 after it. 多大 doesn't take 岁.

duoda.en: How old is your friend this year?
duoda.why: 多大 comes after the time word, right before 了.

zenme.en: How are you getting to Beijing? - By plane.
zenme.why: Asking the way to do something: 怎么 + verb.
怎么 goes directly before the verb.

zenme.en: How do you make this dish?
zenme.why: 怎么 + verb asks how to do it.

zenme.en: How are you getting to the hospital?
zenme.why: 怎么 goes before the verb, not at the end.

zenme.en: How do we get to your place?
zenme.why: 怎么 sits directly before the verb 去.

zenmeyang.why: Asking for an opinion: 怎么样 at the end, with no verb after it.

zenmeyang.en: Let's eat here - how about it?
zenmeyang.why: After a suggestion, 怎么样 at the end means how about it?
Thing + 怎么样 asks what it was like.

zenmeyang.en: How do you write this character?
zenmeyang.why: Before a verb use 怎么; 怎么样 is not followed by a verb.

zenmeyang.en: What's the weather like in Beijing today?
zenmeyang.why: 怎么样 goes at the end, after the thing you ask about.

ne.en: I like cats. What about you?
ne.why: 你呢 bounces the same question back without repeating it.
Thing + 呢 asks where it has gone.

ne.en: I'm going to the shop tomorrow. What about you?
ne.why: After saying something about yourself, 你呢 asks the same of them.

ne.en: I'll have water. How about you?
ne.why: To bounce a question back, use 呢, not 吗.

ne.en: My daughter is eight. And your son?
ne.why: 呢 goes right after the person you are asking about.

hui.ch: 你__说汉语吗？——会，我学习了两年。
hui.en: Can you speak Chinese? - Yes, I studied it for two years.
hui.why: A language is a learned skill, so it takes 会.

hui.en: My mum can speak a little Chinese.
hui.why: 会 comes right before the verb 说.

hui.ch: 我不会做中国菜，我妈妈会。
hui.en: I can't cook Chinese food, but my mum can.
hui.why: Cooking is a learned skill: 会 and 不会.

hui.en: My mum can cook Chinese food.
hui.why: 会 goes before the verb, not after it.
不会 comes as one unit right before the verb.

neng.ch: 老师，我__看一下这本书吗？
neng.en: Teacher, may I have a look at this book?
neng.why: Asking permission takes 能, not the skill word 会.

neng.en: Can you make phone calls here?
neng.why: 能 + verb asks if something is allowed.

neng.ch: 他今天不能来，他在医院。
neng.en: He can't come today - he's in hospital.
neng.why: Circumstances stop him, so it's 不能.
Asking permission takes 能; 会 is for a learned skill.
能 goes right before the verb.

qing.why: 请 + verb makes a polite request.
请 comes first, then the request.

qing.en: I'll treat you to Chinese food.
qing.why: 请 + person + verb can mean it's my treat.
请 goes at the front, before the verb.

qing.en: I'll treat you to a film tomorrow.
qing.why: 请 + person + verb: 请你看电影.

qu-do.en: I'm at home - come over to my place for tea.
qu-do.why: Coming towards the speaker takes 来; the place comes before what you do there.

qu-do.en: I'd like to go to Beijing to study Chinese.
qu-do.why: First go somewhere, then say what you do there.

qu-do.ch: 我朋友来我家吃中国菜。
qu-do.en: My friend is coming to my home to eat Chinese food.
qu-do.why: 来 + place + action, in the order it happens.

qu-do.en: Mum is going to the hospital to see a doctor.
qu-do.why: Going comes first, then what you do there.

qu-do.en: Tomorrow I'm going to a restaurant to eat Chinese food.
qu-do.why: 去 + place comes before the action done there.

time-first.en: I'm working at the hospital tomorrow.
time-first.why: Time, then 在 + place, then the verb.

time-first.ch: 上午我在学校，下午我在家。
time-first.en: In the morning I'm at school; in the afternoon I'm at home.
time-first.why: A time word can open the sentence.
Time comes before place: time + 在 + place + verb.

time-first.en: My mum is working at the hospital today.
time-first.why: The time word goes before 在 + place and the verb.

time-first.en: I'm going shopping at three this afternoon.
time-first.why: Time goes before the verb, and 下午 comes before 三点.

bu-mei.ch: 我昨天__看电视，我去看电影了。
bu-mei.en: I didn't watch TV yesterday - I went to see a film.
bu-mei.why: Something that didn't happen takes 没有, not 不.
没有 goes right before the verb for didn't.

bu-mei.fix: 昨天下午我没有看电视。
bu-mei.en: I didn't watch TV yesterday afternoon.
bu-mei.why: Yesterday didn't happen: use 没有, not 不.
A feeling or habit takes 不, right before the verb.

tai-le.why: The 了 at the end is part of 太……了.

tai-le.ch: 那个商店的东西不太多。
tai-le.en: That shop doesn't have very many things.
tai-le.why: In the negative 不太, the 了 drops.
太 + adjective needs 了 at the end.

tai-le.en: It's so cold in Beijing today!
tai-le.why: 太 goes right before the adjective.

dou.ch: 我爸爸和我妈妈__是医生。
dou.en: My dad and my mum are both doctors.
dou.why: 都 comes after the group and before the verb.

dou.en: My friends can all speak Chinese.
dou.why: 都 stands after the group, before 会 + verb.

dou.en: Not all of them are Chinese.
dou.why: 不都 means not all of them.
都 must go before the verb, never at the end.

dou.en: Yesterday my daughter and I both went to the shop.
dou.why: 都 goes after the whole group, right before the verb.

he.ch: 我想买一个杯子__一本书。
he.en: I'd like to buy a cup and a book.
he.why: 和 joins two nouns: 杯子 and 书.

he.en: Are you and your dad both doctors?
he.why: 和 links two people; 都 then comes before the verb.

he.ch: 我认识你的老师和同学。
he.en: I know your teacher and your classmates.
he.why: 和 joins two nouns after the verb.

he.ch: 我吃米饭和我朋友吃苹果。
he.fix: 我吃米饭，我朋友吃苹果。
he.en: I'm eating rice and my friend is eating an apple.
he.why: 和 can't join two sentences; just put them side by side.

he.en: My cat and dog are both at home.
he.why: 和 stands between the two nouns 猫 and 狗.

measure.en: I want to buy two books.
measure.why: Books take the measure word 本.
Number + measure word + noun: 两个中国朋友.
那 needs a measure word too: 那个杯子.

measure.en: I want to buy this book.
measure.why: 这 needs a measure word before the noun: 这本书.
The measure word goes between 这 and the noun.

numbers.ch: 我有__个女儿，一个八岁，一个五岁。
numbers.en: I have two daughters - one is eight, one is five.
numbers.why: Before a measure word, two is 两, not 二.
Build it like a sum: 九十 + 六 = 96, then the measure word.

numbers.en: My mum is fifty-two this year.
numbers.why: Inside a bigger number, 2 stays 二.
Counting things, 2 becomes 两 before a measure word.

numbers.en: My daughter is eleven this year.
numbers.why: Eleven is ten + one: 十一.

money.why: In speech a price is number + 块.
Ask a price with 多少钱 after the thing.

money.ch: 这个杯子九块，那个十块。
money.en: This cup is nine kuai, that one is ten.
money.why: Number + 块 is a price; 钱 can be left off.
A price needs 块 after the number; 钱 alone is not enough.
块 comes right after the number, before 钱.

dates.en: What day of the week was yesterday?
dates.why: Weekdays are numbered, so ask 星期几.
Big to small: year, month, day, then weekday.

dates.en: I lived in Beijing for a month.
dates.why: 一个月 is a length of time; 一月 would be January.

dates.en: I'm going to Beijing on 10 September.
dates.why: The month comes before the day.
月 comes after the month number, before the day.

clock.en: I watched TV for twenty minutes.
clock.why: How long takes 分钟; 点 tells what time it is.

clock.en: I'm going to the hospital at two tomorrow afternoon.
clock.why: The part of the day comes first: 下午两点, then the verb.

clock.en: Please wait ten minutes for me.
clock.why: A length of time is number + 分钟.

clock.en: I'm going to the shop at ten in the morning.
clock.why: 上午 goes before the hour: 上午十点.
点 comes right after the hour number.

shi-de.en: When did you come to Beijing?
shi-de.why: 是……的 asks about when it happened; the 的 can't be dropped.
是 + the place + verb + 的 puts the spotlight on where.

shi-de.ch: 这个杯子是我女儿买的。
shi-de.why: 是……的 spotlights who did it.
是……的 needs the 的 at the end.

shi-de.en: I came at ten in the morning.
shi-de.why: 的 closes the pattern, right after the verb.

ba-particle.why: 吧 at the end: a guess you expect to be yes.
吧 asks for a guess to be confirmed.
A suggestion takes 吧; 吗 asks a question.

ba-particle.en: Let's sit here for a bit.
ba-particle.why: 吧 goes at the end of the suggestion.

nin-men.why: One teacher, so the polite 您. 你们 is for more than one person.

nin-men.en: Hello, all of you! I'm your teacher.
nin-men.why: The teacher greets the whole class, so 你们.
我们 is the subject, so it comes first.
With a number before it, 朋友 takes no 们.
她们 = they (women): 们 makes 她 more than one.
